text: Which file format is NOT supported for loading data into Snowflake using COPY INTO?

options.A: CSV
options.B: JSON
options.C: Parquet

explanation: Snowflake supports CSV, JSON, Avro, ORC, Parquet, and XML for bulk loading. Excel (.xlsx), PDF, and binary formats are NOT supported. Data must be converted to a supported format before loading.

text: An engineer runs COPY INTO with VALIDATION_MODE = 'RETURN_ALL_ERRORS'. How many rows are loaded into the table?

options.A: All valid rows are loaded; only errors are returned separately
options.B: Zero rows are loaded — VALIDATION_MODE is a dry-run that validates without loading any data
options.C: All rows are loaded, and errors are appended to an error log table
options.D: Only the first 1000 rows are loaded as a test batch

explanation: VALIDATION_MODE performs a dry-run validation of the data files. NO data is loaded regardless of the validation option used. It returns information about errors in the files without modifying the target table.

text: Bulk COPY INTO completes successfully. How long does Snowflake retain the load metadata to prevent duplicate file loading?

options.A: 14 days
options.B: 30 days
options.C: 64 days

explanation: Bulk COPY INTO retains load metadata for 64 days. Snowpipe retains it for 14 days. After retention expires, files are treated as new and could be loaded again if re-staged. FORCE = TRUE bypasses this deduplication.

text: A COPY INTO command uses ON_ERROR = 'SKIP_FILE_3'. A file has exactly 2 errors. What happens?

options.A: The file is skipped because it has errors
options.B: The file is loaded — SKIP_FILE_n skips only when error count >= n, so 2 errors < 3 means the file is processed
options.C: Only the 2 error rows are skipped; all other rows load normally

explanation: SKIP_FILE_n skips a file ONLY when the number of errors >= n. With SKIP_FILE_3, a file with exactly 2 errors does NOT meet the threshold, so the file is processed (valid rows loaded, error rows handled per behavior). A file with 3+ errors would be skipped entirely.

text: An engineer sets PURGE = TRUE and ON_ERROR = 'SKIP_FILE'. One file has errors and is skipped. Is it purged?

options.A: Yes — PURGE deletes all files regardless of load status
options.B: No — files skipped entirely by SKIP_FILE are NOT purged. Only successfully processed files are deleted.
options.C: Yes — but only after 24 hours
options.D: No — PURGE only works with ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE'

explanation: PURGE = TRUE deletes files that were PROCESSED (even partially with CONTINUE). Files that were entirely skipped by SKIP_FILE are NOT purged — they remain on the stage for investigation or retry.

text: An engineer needs to reload a file that was already loaded 10 days ago. The file has the same name and path. What happens with a normal COPY INTO?

options.A: The file is loaded again because Snowflake doesn't track file names
options.B: The file is skipped because load metadata (within the 64-day retention) detects it as already loaded
options.C: The file is loaded but only new rows are inserted
options.D: An error is raised because duplicate files are not allowed

explanation: Snowflake tracks loaded file metadata for 64 days (bulk COPY). Within this window, files with the same name are skipped to prevent duplicates. To force a reload, use FORCE = TRUE (risks duplicates) or rename the file.

text: Which TWO statements about the PUT command are TRUE? (Select TWO)

options.A: PUT works from the Snowsight web UI
options.B: PUT uploads files from the local filesystem to internal stages only
options.C: PUT auto-compresses files with GZIP by default (AUTO_COMPRESS = TRUE)
options.D: PUT can upload directly to external stages like S3

explanation: PUT: (1) uploads from local filesystem to INTERNAL stages only (not external), and (2) auto-compresses with GZIP by default. PUT does NOT work from Snowsight (browser has no filesystem access) and does NOT upload to external stages. No special role is required beyond stage privileges.

text: What does the METADATA$FILENAME pseudo-column return when used in a COPY INTO SELECT statement?

options.A: The target table name where data will be loaded
options.B: The source filename from the stage that the current row was loaded from
options.C: The internal Snowflake file ID for tracking
options.D: The file format type (CSV, JSON, etc.)

explanation: METADATA$FILENAME returns the name of the source file from the stage. METADATA$FILE_ROW_NUMBER returns the row number within that file. These pseudo-columns are only available in COPY INTO with a SELECT (transform) clause.

text: Multiple file format options are specified at different levels: inline in COPY INTO, at the stage level, and at the schema level. Which takes precedence?

options.A: Schema-level defaults always override
options.B: Stage-level file format takes highest precedence
options.C: COPY INTO inline options take highest precedence, then stage-level, then schema/database defaults

explanation: File format precedence: COPY INTO inline > stage-level > schema/database defaults. The most specific (inline) setting wins, similar to Snowflake's general parameter hierarchy.

text: An engineer wants to unload data from a table into an external stage, splitting the output files by the REGION column. Which COPY INTO option achieves this?

options.A: GROUP BY (REGION)
options.B: PARTITION BY (REGION)
options.C: SPLIT BY (REGION)

explanation: PARTITION BY splits unloaded data into separate files based on column values. Each unique value of the specified column creates a separate output path/file. This is used for COPY INTO @stage (unload direction only).

text: What is the default ON_ERROR behavior for Snowpipe?

options.A: ABORT_STATEMENT — stop on first error
options.B: SKIP_FILE — skip files with errors and continue loading other files
options.C: CONTINUE — skip bad rows and load valid rows from all files

explanation: Snowpipe default ON_ERROR = SKIP_FILE. Bulk COPY INTO default = ABORT_STATEMENT. This is one of the most common exam traps — knowing which default applies to which method.

text: An engineer creates a pipe with AUTO_INGEST = TRUE pointing to an S3 bucket. What cloud service does Snowflake use to receive file arrival notifications from S3?

options.A: AWS Lambda
options.B: Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service)
options.C: AWS Kinesis

explanation: For S3 auto-ingest, Snowflake creates and manages an SQS queue. S3 event notifications are sent to this SQS queue, which Snowpipe monitors. The SQS queue ARN is visible via SHOW PIPES (notification_channel column). SNS can be used as an intermediary but SQS is the endpoint.

text: Snowpipe processes files using compute resources. Whose virtual warehouse is used?

options.A: The warehouse specified in the pipe definition
options.B: The SYSADMIN default warehouse
options.C: Snowflake-managed serverless compute — Snowpipe does NOT use a user warehouse
options.D: The warehouse of the user who created the pipe

explanation: Snowpipe uses Snowflake-managed serverless compute. It does NOT require or use any user-provisioned virtual warehouse. Credits are billed based on actual compute used, at a per-second rate. Pipes do not have a WAREHOUSE parameter.

text: Snowpipe retains load metadata for how long?

options.A: 64 days (same as bulk COPY)
options.B: 14 days — after which files may be loaded again if re-staged
options.C: 7 days
options.D: Indefinitely until the pipe is dropped

explanation: Snowpipe retains file load metadata for 14 days. Bulk COPY retains it for 64 days. After 14 days, Snowpipe treats the same file as new if it reappears. This is a key difference tested on exams.

text: How does Snowpipe Streaming differ from file-based Snowpipe?

options.A: Snowpipe Streaming uses larger batch files for better throughput
options.B: Snowpipe Streaming inserts rows DIRECTLY via the Ingest SDK without staging files — providing lower latency
options.C: Snowpipe Streaming requires a dedicated warehouse
options.D: Snowpipe Streaming only works with JSON data

explanation: Snowpipe Streaming (via the Ingest SDK) inserts rows directly into Snowflake internal buffers WITHOUT staging files first. This provides lower latency than file-based Snowpipe. Rows are asynchronously migrated to micro-partitions.

text: A stream on a table tracks changes. An INSERT of 5 rows is committed, then 2 of those rows are deleted, all before the stream is consumed. When the stream is queried, how many net INSERT records appear?

options.A: 5 — all inserts are recorded regardless of subsequent deletes
options.B: 3 — a standard stream provides the NET delta (5 inserts - 2 deletes = 3 net inserts)
options.C: 7 — 5 inserts + 2 deletes shown separately

explanation: A standard (delta) stream provides the MINIMAL net change set between two offsets. Rows inserted then deleted before consumption cancel out in the delta — they don't appear. The stream shows only the 3 rows that exist as net new inserts.

text: A stream's offset has not been advanced for a long period. The stream becomes stale. How can it be fixed?

options.A: Run ALTER STREAM ... REFRESH to reset the offset
options.B: The stale stream cannot be recovered — it must be DROPPED and RECREATED
options.C: Run SYSTEM$STREAM_REPAIR() to rebuild the offset
options.D: Wait 24 hours for Snowflake to auto-recover the stream

explanation: A stale stream cannot be repaired or refreshed. It must be dropped (DROP STREAM) and recreated (CREATE STREAM). Staleness occurs when the stream offset falls outside the data retention period for the source table.

text: What determines when a stream becomes stale?

options.A: When 14 days pass without consumption
options.B: When the stream offset falls outside the GREATER of DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS and MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS
options.C: When the source table exceeds 1 TB
options.D: When more than 1 million changes accumulate

explanation: A stream becomes stale when its offset is older than the greater of DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS and MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS for the source table. Snowflake extends retention temporarily to prevent staleness, but if unconsumed too long, the stream goes stale.

text: A task uses WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('my_stream'). The stream has no changes since last consumption. What happens when the task's schedule fires?

options.A: The task runs but processes zero rows
options.B: The task is SKIPPED entirely — WHEN clause evaluates to FALSE, consuming zero compute
options.C: The task runs and errors because the stream is empty

explanation: When the WHEN clause evaluates to FALSE (no data in stream), the task is SKIPPED entirely. No warehouse is resumed, no compute is consumed. This is a cost-saving pattern for event-driven processing.

text: What privilege is required to resume or suspend a task?

options.A: OWNERSHIP on the task
options.B: OPERATE privilege on the task
options.C: EXECUTE TASK privilege on the account

explanation: The OPERATE privilege allows a role to resume, suspend, or manually execute a task. OWNERSHIP provides full control. EXECUTE TASK is an account-level privilege needed for the task to actually run, but OPERATE is needed for resume/suspend.

text: A serverless task is created without specifying a WAREHOUSE. What parameter controls the initial compute size?

options.A: WAREHOUSE_SIZE
options.B: USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE
options.C: SERVERLESS_COMPUTE_POOL

explanation: Serverless tasks use Snowflake-managed compute. USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE sets the starting compute size. Snowflake can auto-scale from there based on workload. No user warehouse is provisioned.

text: A task has ALLOW_OVERLAPPING_EXECUTION = FALSE (default). The previous run is still executing when the next scheduled time arrives. What happens?

options.A: A second instance starts in parallel
options.B: The new run is SKIPPED — it will not execute until the current run finishes and the next schedule fires
options.C: The current run is cancelled and the new one starts
options.D: Both runs are queued and executed sequentially

explanation: With ALLOW_OVERLAPPING_EXECUTION = FALSE (default), if a task is still running when its next scheduled execution time arrives, the new run is skipped. This prevents overlapping executions and potential resource contention.

text: A dynamic table is defined with TARGET_LAG = '10 minutes'. A query joins three source tables. Can the dynamic table perform this JOIN?

options.A: No — dynamic tables are limited to single-table queries like materialized views
options.B: Yes — dynamic tables support JOINs, aggregations, and multi-table queries (unlike materialized views)
options.C: Yes, but only with FULL refresh mode
options.D: No — JOINs require streams and tasks instead

explanation: Dynamic tables support JOINs, aggregations, window functions, and multi-table queries. This is a key advantage over materialized views (single table only). Dynamic tables can use either INCREMENTAL or FULL refresh mode for joins.

text: What does TARGET_LAG = 'DOWNSTREAM' mean for a dynamic table?

options.A: The table refreshes based on downstream consumer lag requirements — it has no independent schedule
options.B: The table only refreshes when queried directly
options.C: The table refreshes every downstream table first

explanation: TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM means the dynamic table has no independent refresh schedule. It refreshes only when a downstream dynamic table (one that reads from it) triggers a refresh. Snowflake derives timing from the shortest target lag among downstream consumers.

text: What is the minimum allowed TARGET_LAG for a dynamic table?

options.A: 1 second
options.B: 30 seconds
options.C: 60 seconds (1 minute)

explanation: The minimum TARGET_LAG for a dynamic table is 60 seconds (1 minute). Values below this fail validation. For sub-minute freshness, use materialized views (always current) or streams and tasks.

text: Can you run INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE directly on a dynamic table?

options.A: Yes — dynamic tables behave like regular tables
options.B: No — dynamic tables are READ-ONLY. Their content is entirely determined by the defining SELECT query.
options.C: Yes, but only DELETE for GDPR compliance
options.D: Yes, if the table uses FULL refresh mode

explanation: Dynamic tables are read-only. You cannot run INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE against them. Their content is exclusively determined by the defining SELECT query. For DML needs, use streams and tasks with standard tables.

text: Which TWO types of stream are available in Snowflake? (Select TWO)

options.A: Standard (delta) — tracks inserts, updates, and deletes as net changes
options.B: Append-only — tracks row inserts only, ignoring updates and deletes
options.C: Delete-only — tracks only row deletions
options.D: Full-history — tracks all historical versions of every row
options.E: Trigger-based — fires a callback function on each change

explanation: Snowflake supports: Standard (delta) streams that track all DML as net changes, Append-only streams that track inserts only, and Insert-only streams (for external/Iceberg tables). There are no delete-only, full-history, or trigger-based stream types.

text: A stream is consumed within a DML transaction. The transaction is then rolled back. What happens to the stream offset?

options.A: The offset advances regardless of the transaction outcome
options.B: The offset does NOT advance — it only advances on successful transaction COMMIT
options.C: The offset advances but the consumed data is replayed on next query

explanation: Stream offsets only advance when consumed in a DML transaction that successfully commits. If the transaction rolls back, the stream offset remains at its previous position, and the same change records are available for the next consumption.

text: Does querying a stream (SELECT * FROM my_stream) without a DML wrapper advance its offset?

options.A: Yes — any query against the stream advances the offset
options.B: No — querying alone does NOT advance the offset. Only consumption within a DML transaction advances it.
options.C: Yes, but only if the query returns more than 100 rows

explanation: Simply querying a stream (SELECT) does NOT advance its offset. The offset advances ONLY when stream data is consumed in a DML statement (INSERT INTO, MERGE, CTAS, COPY INTO location) within a successfully committed transaction.

text: A storage integration is created for an S3 bucket. Does the integration store AWS access keys or secret keys?

options.A: Yes — the integration securely stores encrypted AWS credentials
options.B: No — the integration stores an IAM user ARN. The customer grants trust via an IAM role policy in AWS.
options.C: Yes — but only the access key, not the secret
options.D: No — credentials are passed inline with each query

explanation: Storage integrations do NOT store access keys or secrets. They store a Snowflake IAM user ARN and external ID. The customer creates an IAM role in AWS and grants the Snowflake IAM user permission to assume it. This eliminates inline credentials.

text: Which integration type is used to authenticate Snowflake with cloud storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS) without passing inline credentials?

options.A: API integration
options.B: Storage integration
options.C: Notification integration

explanation: Storage integrations establish a trust relationship between Snowflake and cloud storage (S3/Azure/GCS). They use IAM roles (AWS), service principals (Azure), or service accounts (GCS) instead of inline credentials. STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS restricts accessible paths.

text: An engineer loads a JSON file with an outer array: [{...}, {...}, {...}]. Without any special options, each row in the target table contains the ENTIRE array. What file format option fixes this?

options.A: FLATTEN_ARRAY = TRUE
options.B: STRIP_OUTER_ARRAY = TRUE — removes the outer brackets so each element becomes one row
options.C: ARRAY_TO_ROWS = TRUE

explanation: STRIP_OUTER_ARRAY = TRUE removes the outer [ ] from a JSON file, treating each top-level array element as a separate row. Without this option, the entire array is loaded as a single VARIANT value in one row.

text: What is the difference between SKIP_HEADER and PARSE_HEADER in CSV file format options?

options.A: They are identical — both skip the first row
options.B: SKIP_HEADER skips N rows (discards them). PARSE_HEADER reads the first row as column names for MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME.
options.C: PARSE_HEADER skips multiple rows; SKIP_HEADER skips only one
options.D: SKIP_HEADER is for CSV; PARSE_HEADER is for JSON

explanation: SKIP_HEADER = N simply discards the first N rows without using them. PARSE_HEADER = TRUE reads the first row to extract column names, enabling MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME to map file columns to table columns by name instead of position.

text: An engineer creates an external stage pointing to s3://mybucket/data/. What does a directory table on this stage provide?

options.A: The actual data content of each file in columnar format
options.B: File-level metadata: URLs, file sizes, timestamps, and ETags — NOT the data content
options.C: A queryable replica of the S3 bucket

explanation: Directory tables provide file-level metadata on stages: file URLs, sizes, last modified timestamps, and ETags. They do NOT contain the actual data content. They are useful for discovery and building dynamic ingestion pipelines.

text: A pipe with AUTO_INGEST = TRUE has been paused for 20 days. What happens to event notifications received during this period?

options.A: All notifications are queued indefinitely and processed when the pipe resumes
options.B: Notifications are retained for 14 days only. The pipe is considered stale and notifications older than 14 days may be lost.
options.C: Notifications are immediately discarded when the pipe is paused
options.D: Notifications are forwarded to a dead-letter queue

explanation: When a pipe is paused, event messages are retained for a limited period (14 days by default). If paused longer than 14 days, the pipe is considered stale. Notifications older than 14 days may be dropped. On resume, Snowpipe processes remaining messages on a best-effort basis.

text: Multiple consumers need to process the same change data from a table independently. What is the recommended approach?

options.A: Create a single stream and have all consumers read from it
options.B: Create a SEPARATE stream for each consumer — each stream maintains its own independent offset
options.C: Use a shared materialized view for all consumers
options.D: Use CHANGES clause for all consumers

explanation: Each stream maintains its own offset. When one consumer advances the offset via DML, the data is gone for that stream. To allow independent consumption, create separate streams per consumer. Streams only store offsets (no data duplication), so multiple streams are cheap.

text: An append-only stream is created on a table. 10 rows are inserted, then 5 of those rows are deleted before the stream is consumed. How many records does the append-only stream show?

options.A: 5 (net inserts after deletes)
options.B: 10 — append-only streams track inserts ONLY and ignore deletes
options.C: 15 (10 inserts + 5 deletes)

explanation: Append-only streams exclusively track row INSERTS. Updates, deletes, and truncates are NOT captured. Even though 5 rows were deleted, the append-only stream still shows all 10 original inserts. This makes append-only streams more performant for ELT scenarios.

text: The Kafka connector for Snowflake ingests streaming data. What authentication method does it use to connect to Snowflake?

options.A: Username and password stored in the connector config
options.B: Key-pair (RSA) authentication
options.C: OAuth with refresh tokens

explanation: The Snowflake Kafka connector uses key-pair (RSA) authentication for programmatic, non-interactive access. The private key is configured in the connector properties, and the corresponding public key is registered in Snowflake for the service user.

text: What function can you use to detect the schema (column names and types) of files in a stage BEFORE loading them?

options.A: DESCRIBE STAGE
options.B: INFER_SCHEMA(location, format) — detects file schema for planning COPY operations
options.C: PARSE_FILE()

explanation: INFER_SCHEMA detects column names, types, and order from staged files (Parquet, ORC, Avro, CSV with PARSE_HEADER). This allows creating tables with matching schemas before loading. DESCRIBE STAGE shows stage properties, not file schemas.

text: Which TWO statements about dynamic tables vs materialized views are TRUE? (Select TWO)

options.A: Materialized views support JOINs; dynamic tables do not
options.B: Dynamic tables support JOINs; materialized views are limited to single-table queries
options.C: Materialized views are always current (no lag); dynamic tables have a minimum TARGET_LAG of 1 minute
options.D: Dynamic tables can be directly updated with INSERT statements
options.E: Materialized views are available in Standard Edition

explanation: Dynamic tables: support JOINs/aggregations, minimum 1-minute lag, read-only. Materialized views: single-table only, always current (optimizer auto-rewrites queries), Enterprise+ required. Dynamic tables are the preferred approach for multi-table pipelines.
